group.name: Post-Industrial Collapse
group.tagline: Our civilisation ends in a single generation, and the survivors inherit the ruins.
group.question: What grows in the wreckage of the industrial world?
group.divergenceMechanism: A discrete catastrophe inside the 20th or 21st century destroys the industrial order.

lineages.title: A Canticle for Leibowitz
lineages.creator: Walter M. Miller Jr.

divergence.label: The Flame Deluge
divergence.delta: Real: 1962 — the Cuban Missile Crisis ends in a withdrawal and a telephone hotline, and the war that the century spent preparing for does not come. Fiction: it comes, and then the survivors turn on the knowledge that made it.

sources.title: Wikipedia: A Canticle for Leibowitz — the Flame Deluge and the Simplification; the novel gives no year for either

divergence.note: Miller never puts a calendar year on the war. The novel was written in the late 1950s and its pre-war world is plainly the one its first readers lived in — Leibowitz is a Jewish electrical engineer working for the United States military, and the war is the one everybody expected. 1962 is chosen as the year that expectation came closest to being met, and the divergence note says so rather than implying the book dates it. The three parts that follow are six centuries apart, which the novel states; the second part is conventionally dated to 3174, the date the Japanese edition took for its title, and the other two follow from it.

ending.why: The species escapes to the stars and the Earth is burned again behind it — the same ending the book opened with, which is the whole argument it is making.

events.title: The Flame Deluge
events.description: The nuclear exchange the century had been preparing for happens. Cities burn, the fallout drifts, and the states that fought it stop existing as states; what is left of the twentieth century is ruins, radiation and survivors who remember who did it.

sources.title: Wikipedia: A Canticle for Leibowitz (the war and the backlash that follows)

events.note: The novel does not date the war; it is placed here in the year the crisis over Cuba nearly produced it, and the divergence field records that this is a choice. The story's own anchor is that its pre-war world is the reader's.
events.binWhy: The nuclear war that our 1962 avoided is fought.

facets.change: armed peace → global nuclear exchange

events.title: The Simplification
events.description: The survivors turn on the thing that caused it. Mobs calling themselves Simpletons burn libraries and kill anyone who can read; by the end of it illiteracy is near-total and the accumulated knowledge of the species exists only in what a few people could carry in their heads or hide.

sources.title: Wikipedia: A Canticle for Leibowitz (the Simplification)

events.note: The novel describes the Simplification as following the war but never dates it; the span is set here at about a decade after, which is as much as the book supports. What it states plainly is the mechanism: the learned were killed, and books were burned.
events.binWhy: The survivors destroy the knowledge that built the weapons.

facets.change: a literate world → an illiterate one, deliberately

events.title: The Albertian Order of Leibowitz
events.description: A survivor who was an engineer before the war becomes a monk, and asks the Church for permission to found an order whose work is to hide books, copy them and remember them. Its abbey stands in the New Mexico desert, on a road that used to run from the Great Salt Lake to El Paso.
events.note: The founding follows the Simplification and precedes Leibowitz's martyrdom; the novel gives no years for either. The order's purpose is the one fact that matters here and it is stated directly.
events.binWhy: An order is founded to preserve what the burning left.

facets.change: knowledge destroyed → knowledge hidden and copied

events.title: A novice finds the fallout shelter
events.description: Six hundred years later a novice sheltering from wolves uncovers a buried fallout shelter holding handwritten notes and a shopping list on a memo pad. He spends fifteen years illuminating a copy of them, the order argues over whether the relics are genuine, and the Church eventually makes the engineer a saint.

sources.title: Wikipedia: A Canticle for Leibowitz (the three parts are six centuries apart)

events.note: The novel states that the abbey still keeps its Memorabilia 'six hundred years after his death'; it does not print the year. 2574 is that interval measured from the founding, and the Japanese edition's title dates this part to the 26th century, which agrees.
events.binWhy: The buried record of the old world is found and read.

facets.change: a buried shelter → a relic that makes a saint

events.title: The new Renaissance rediscovers the atom
events.description: Six hundred years on, the world has states again, and the scholars of the new civilisation work through the Memorabilia until they can do what the old one did. The first thing they rebuild is the weapon, and the Church that kept the knowledge alive watches it happen.

sources.title: Wikipedia: A Canticle for Leibowitz (the second part; 3174 is the Japanese edition's title date)

events.note: This is the second part, which the novel places six centuries after the first. The 3174 date is the one the Japanese edition used as its title; the book itself says only 'six hundred years later'.
events.binWhy: The recovered knowledge reaches nuclear weapons again.

facets.change: a rebuilt civilisation → one that can destroy itself again

events.title: The starship leaves, and the Earth burns again
events.description: As the second nuclear war begins, the Church loads a starship with monks, archives and a colony and launches it. The ship gets away; the planet behind it does not, and the last thing the book says is that the cycle has closed exactly where it started.
events.note: The third part, again six centuries after the second. The novel ends with the launch and the war, in that order, and the point of the ending is that it repeats the first.
events.binWhy: A colony ship escapes a second nuclear war.

facets.change: a world about to end → a species leaving it

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs here because its fork is a war, not an invention, and its own history is the subject: the twentieth century ends the way the century feared, and everything after is the slow rebuilding and the second collapse. Tier coverage is T3 for the war, the burning and the founding (1962-1980) and T1 for the three six-century parts (2574, 3174, 3781); there is no T2 because the novel jumps from the decade after the war straight to the twenty-sixth century, and no T4 because its history begins in living memory.

lineages.title: Planet of the Apes
lineages.creator: Franklin J. Schaffner (dir.); Michael Wilson & Rod Serling (screenplay), from Pierre Boulle's novel

divergence.label: The plague that kills every dog and cat
divergence.delta: Real: 1983 passes with the world's pets alive and the West rearming; nothing has ended. Fiction: a global plague kills every dog and cat on Earth within months, humans adopt apes as pets and then as slaves, and within a generation the apes have taken the planet.
divergence.note: The pentalogy's first impossible event is actually 1973, when Zira and Cornelius arrive from the destroyed future and Caesar is born, but that is a closed bootstrap loop rather than a break in human history. 1983 is Conquest's 'eight years' before its 1991 uprising and is the first dated alteration to human civilisation; the revolt (1991) and the undated nuclear war are downstream. Confidence is medium because the film supplies only the relative 'eight years ago', not a year.

ending.why: The astronaut finds the ruins of New York; humanity blew itself up and the apes inherited the Earth.

events.title: On the Origin of Species
events.description: Real history, not fiction: Darwin publishes natural selection, the idea this series literalises by putting apes on top of the pile.
events.note: Real-world background; the fiction itself is silent before 1972.
events.binWhy: A discovery the rest of the history grows from.

facets.change: fixed species → natural selection published

events.title: The Icarus leaves Earth
events.description: Taylor's ANSA mission launches into the film's own near future, and relativistic time dilation will carry the crew 2,006 years forward while only eighteen months pass for them.
events.note: No on-screen date card. 1972 is derived from the 3978 arrival minus the 2,006 elapsed years the crew log, and from Landon's line about 'the class of '72'.
events.binWhy: A first mission leaves for territory nobody has reached.

facets.change: Earth → a mission flung two thousand years forward

events.title: Zira and Cornelius land in their own past
events.description: The chimpanzees who fled the destroyed Earth arrive in a recognisable 1973 Los Angeles, testify before a congressional committee and are killed, but their son Caesar survives to close the series' bootstrap loop.
events.note: The first impossible event in the series, but a closed causal loop rather than a change to human history, which is why this lineage's fork is placed at the 1983 plague instead.
events.binWhy: Someone or something arrives out of its own time and changes the present.

facets.change: the present → visited by talking apes from a destroyed future

events.title: The plague that kills every dog and cat
events.description: A global plague wipes out the world's dogs and cats within months, humans take apes into their homes as replacements, and the species that will inherit the planet becomes first a pet and then property.
events.note: Conquest gives only the relative 'eight years ago' before its 1991 uprising, so 1983 is arithmetic; the same film is frequently misreported as being set in 1983.
events.binWhy: A disease or biological failure strikes on a mass scale.

facets.change: pets → all dead; apes brought into homes

events.title: Caesar's ape uprising
events.description: The enslaved apes of North America revolt and take the cities, and the human industrial order begins to come apart inside a single generation.
events.note: Conquest's title card gives 1991 and the internal arithmetic fits (Caesar is eighteen, born in 1973), though some timelines read the film as 1993.
events.binWhy: The ruled revolt against those who hold power over them.

facets.change: enslaved apes → take the cities

events.title: The war that ravages the surface
events.description: The human counter-attack becomes the 'vilest war in human history' and leaves the surface a radioactive ruin, which is the world of the Forbidden Zone that Taylor will find.
events.note: Never dated on screen: Battle's Lawgiver places it in the aftermath of Caesar's victory, and that film's 'twelve-year truce' points to about 1992.
events.binWhy: The counter-attack leaves the surface a radioactive ruin.

facets.change: revolt → the counter-attack leaves the surface a ruin

events.title: Ape City and the truce
events.description: A generation after the revolt, Caesar rules a walled ape city where humans and apes are supposed to be equal, and a narrator six centuries later looks back on how fragile that peace was.
events.note: Battle states no year; 'ten years after a worldwide series of ape revolutions and a brutal nuclear war' plus the twelve-year truce puts the main story around 2003, while some sources prefer 2001.
events.binWhy: A truce between species, and a city built on it.

facets.change: war → a walled city and a fragile truce

events.title: The Lawgiver's history lesson
events.description: In 2670 an ape Lawgiver teaches schoolchildren that humans and apes once lived together, which is the ape world's founding myth and the proof that the human past has become scripture.
events.note: On-screen title card 'North America - 2670 A.D.'; the closing line's '600 years after Caesar's death' contradicts the main story's roughly 2003 setting and is unexplained.
events.binWhy: A jump forward shows what the world became.

facets.change: history → taught as scripture

events.title: Two astronauts crash into ape-ruled America
events.description: The 1974 television series drops a pair of twentieth-century astronauts, launched in 1980, into an ape-ruled North America four centuries after the Lawgiver, where humans are mute livestock and fugitives.
events.note: The date is a chronometer reading that the series itself says may have stopped mid-flight; the 1975 animated series is undated, with fans split between 3479 and 3979.
events.binWhy: Twentieth-century astronauts arrive in a future that is not theirs.

facets.change: the present → astronauts land in an ape-ruled future

events.title: Brent arrives and the doomsday bomb ends the Earth
events.description: A second astronaut follows Taylor's trajectory and, days later, the mutant humans of the Forbidden Zone detonate the Alpha-Omega bomb and destroy the planet.
events.note: Brent states 3955 in dialogue while Taylor's chronometer in the 1968 film reads 3978; the standard rationalisation is that Brent's chronometer was damaged.
events.binWhy: An attack or disaster kills on a scale that remakes society.

facets.change: a ruined world → destroyed outright

events.title: Taylor lands on the ape-ruled Earth
events.description: The 1968 film's frame closes as Taylor's ship comes down in the Forbidden Zone, he is hunted and rendered mute, and the half-buried Statue of Liberty reveals that this planet was always Earth.
events.note: The ship's on-screen chronometer reads 3978; the 'November 25' date comes from a later novelisation, not from the film.
events.binWhy: The half-buried statue tells him where he has been all along.

facets.change: a strange planet → recognised as home

lineages.groupingNote: The pentalogy is this archetype's purest long form: a catastrophe inside the twentieth century ends the human industrial order, and the films then live inside its ruins, from a Statue of Liberty on a beach to a sacred scroll that remembers humans as vermin. The fork is placed at the 1983 plague rather than the 1991 uprising because 1983 is the first dated change to human history; the revolt, the war and ape rule are all downstream of it, while the series' earlier impossible event, Zira and Cornelius arriving in 1973, is a closed bootstrap loop rather than a break in human history. Tiers: T4 and T2 are nearly empty because the fiction jumps from the 1990s straight to 2670; the only T4 entry is real-world background (Darwin, 1859) and the only T2 entry is Battle's roughly 2003 setting. T1 is where this branch actually lives, at 2670, 3085, 3955 and 3978. The 2011-2017 reboot (Rise, Dawn, War) and Kingdom (2024) are a separate continuity that re-runs the collapse as a 2016 laboratory accident and a simian-flu pandemic, and the 2001 Burton film is a third; neither is mixed into the events above.

lineages.title: Mad Max
lineages.creator: George Miller & Byron Kennedy

divergence.label: The oil war
divergence.delta: Real: the 1983 oil glut collapses prices, the West recovers and Australia is a stable democracy. Fiction: the same fuel crisis becomes an unending war for the last petrol, and by December 1984 the highways are held by the last police squad while the institutions behind them fail.
divergence.note: Never stated on screen. The date comes from the official Mad Max 2 production preamble, which describes Iran striking Saudi Arabia and the oil majors failing, reinforced by the Main Force Patrol's 'est. 1983' plate; the first film's own signage reads 6 December 1984 and its title card says only 'a few years from now'. Later material makes it worse: the 2015 Fury Road comics place their own Fall in the 2010s and George Miller says the films have no strict chronology, so the 1980s dating belongs to the flagship trilogy rather than to the franchise.

ending.why: One citadel is freed and its water released, but the wasteland is the world now and a generation has known nothing else.

events.title: The first commercial oil well
events.description: Real history, not fiction: Drake's well at Titusville starts the oil age whose exhaustion this franchise turns into the end of the world.
events.note: Real-world background.
events.binWhy: A discovery the rest of the history grows from.

facets.change: no oil industry → the oil age begins

events.title: The first oil shock
events.description: Real history, not fiction: the OPEC embargo quadruples the price of oil and shows that the industrial West can be brought to its knees by fuel, which is the real crisis the fiction escalates into permanent war.
events.note: Real-world background; the fiction's own oil war is dated only in production and tie-in material.
events.binWhy: A financial or resource shock opens a lasting crisis.

facets.change: cheap oil → an embargo quadruples the price

events.title: Mad Max: 'a few years from now'
events.description: The film is released with a title card that places it a few years ahead of its audience: the Main Force Patrol still answers calls, but the highways are already a war zone and the institutions behind them are failing.
events.note: Australian release 12 April 1979; the on-screen title card is the first film's only firm dating gesture.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The oil war
events.description: The war for the last fuel begins as Iran strikes Saudi Arabia, the Gulf fields burn and the oil majors fail, and the industrial order starts to come apart at the edges.
events.note: Never stated on screen; see the divergence note. The Mad Max 2 narration does not date the collapse at all, and the often-quoted 'last years of the 20th century' line does not exist in the film.
events.binWhy: A major war starts.

facets.change: the last fuel → war for it; the oil majors fail

events.title: The last patrol
events.description: The first film's own date, from the Highway 9 sign: Max hunts Toecutter's gang along a coast where the rule of law now depends on a handful of cars.
events.note: On-screen background signage gives 6 December 1984, the franchise's hardest in-universe date.
events.binWhy: The rule of law now depends on a handful of cars.

facets.change: the rule of law → depends on a handful of cars

events.title: The Road Warrior and the last refinery
events.description: Three years on, the wars have gone nuclear: Max trades a tanker of fuel for a tribe of survivors so they can reach the coast, and the world of the first film is gone.
events.note: The three-year gap comes from the official production preamble, not the film; whether the nuclear exchange happens here or between the first two films depends on which continuity you follow.
events.binWhy: The wars have gone nuclear and the world of three years earlier is gone.

facets.change: fuel wars → gone nuclear; the old world gone

events.title: Bartertown and the children of the Crack in the Earth
events.description: Fifteen years after the fuel wars, Sydney is a ruin, a methane town settles its disputes in the Thunderdome, and a tribe of children waits for the pilot who left them in 1999.
events.note: The fifteen-year gap comes from co-writer Terry Hayes (Starlog, June 1985); the film states no year.
events.binWhy: A permanent settlement or base is founded.

facets.change: ruins → a methane town with its own law

events.title: Fury Road: the wasteland a generation on
events.description: The franchise's furthest era: a citadel trades water for fuel and chrome, a war rig runs for the green place, and Max's forced tattoo records the day count of a life spent in the wreckage.
events.note: Miller: the apocalypse 'happens, and you wind up 45-50 years in the future' from a rolling 'next Wednesday'; the tattoo implies about thirty-three years since the Fall; the 2015 comics put their Fall in the 2010s. The year is arithmetic on Miller's figure, not a stated date. Furiosa (2024) runs the fifteen years directly into this film.
events.binWhy: A jump forward shows what the world became.

facets.change: wasteland → a citadel trading water for fuel

lineages.groupingNote: Mad Max is the archetype stripped to fuel: the world does not end in a war anyone wins, it runs out of oil, and everything after the first film is set among the wreckage of ordinary Australian life, a police interceptor, a refinery, a ruined Sydney. The fork is dated 1983 with low confidence because the collapse is described only in production and tie-in material, while the films' own dating runs from a title card reading 'a few years from now' to on-screen signage reading 6 December 1984. Tiers: this branch has no T1 and never will, because the franchise's furthest era is the Fury Road wasteland roughly forty-five to fifty years past its Fall, so Mad Max simply stops inside our own next century; the T4 entry is real-world background only (the oil age, 1859), and everything the fiction itself depicts from 1973 onward sits in T3 or T2. Miller's repeated insistence that the films have no strict chronology is the honest summary of this lineage's dates.

lineages.title: Twelve Monkeys
lineages.creator: Terry Gilliam (dir.); David & Janet Peoples (screenplay), from Chris Marker's La Jetée

divergence.label: The virus is released in Philadelphia
divergence.delta: Real: the winter of 1996 passes with no plague and five billion people live out their lives. Fiction: on 13 December 1996 a laboratory-grown virus is released in Philadelphia, and by 2035 the survivors are sealed underground, sending prisoners back to change a past that cannot be changed.
divergence.note: The 2035 scientists state the date on screen, describing the release as 'probably on December 13, 1996', with symptoms first detected in Philadelphia on 27 December; the film's opening card says five billion will die in 1997.

ending.why: The plague happens exactly as remembered; the loop closes, five billion die, and the survivors live underground.

events.title: The Russian flu pandemic
events.description: Real history, not fiction: a respiratory pandemic rides the new railway and steamship networks out of Central Asia and kills about a million people, the real rehearsal for the fiction's plague.
events.note: Real-world background; death tolls vary by source.
events.binWhy: A disease or biological failure strikes on a mass scale.

facets.change: new railways → a pandemic rides them

events.title: The first jump lands in the First World War
events.description: A targeting error drops Cole into a trench in 1917, where he is shot in the leg, a wound that will still be in his thigh when he reaches 1996.
events.note: On screen; the bullet is the object half of the film's time loop.
events.binWhy: Someone or something arrives out of its own time and changes the present.

facets.change: a trench → a man from the future lands in it

events.title: La Jetée
events.description: Chris Marker's photo-roman tells the same story with no dates at all, a man from a post-war underground sent back to a woman on a pier, and gives Gilliam's film its structure and its ending.
events.note: Real-world publication; La Jetée never dates its Third World War or its future.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The second jump lands in 1990
events.description: Sent to 1996, Cole arrives six years early, is arrested, and meets Jeffrey Goines and Dr Railly in a Baltimore asylum, seeding the false lead that runs through the rest of the film.
events.note: Railly states 'This is 1990'; the opening title card is dated 12 April 1990.
events.binWhy: Someone or something arrives out of its own time and changes the present.

facets.change: an asylum → a man from the future, six years early

events.title: The virus is released, and the loop closes
events.description: Cole's jump lands in November 1996 and in December he is shot dead at Philadelphia airport in front of his own child self while Dr Peters walks onto a plane carrying the virus, so the plague is not prevented but caused.
events.note: The 2035 scientists state the release date on screen; the Army of the Twelve Monkeys, whose name they blame, are animal-rights activists and a red herring, and the carrier is Goines's assistant, Dr Peters.
events.binWhy: The virus is released; the plague is caused, not prevented.

facets.change: a plan to prevent → the virus released, the loop closed

events.title: Five billion dead
events.description: Within a year the virus has reached every continent and killed about five billion people, the survivors seal themselves into underground compounds, and the industrial world above is finished.
events.note: The opening title card states that five billion people will die in 1997, and the film's ending confirms the outbreak is not averted.
events.binWhy: A disease or biological failure strikes on a mass scale.

facets.change: release → five billion dead within a year

events.title: The underground future
events.description: The film's frame: Philadelphia is a sealed compound, dissidents are volunteered to the time programme, and scientists watch Cole's life on a screen while still trying to recover a pure sample of the original virus.
events.note: 2035 is the standard citation and matches the film's 'thirty years' dialogue loosely; the year is never spoken on screen, and a strict reading of the dialogue implies about 2026.
events.binWhy: A jump forward shows what the world became.

facets.change: the surface → sealed compounds; dissidents sent back

lineages.groupingNote: Twelve Monkeys is this archetype in its bleakest form: a plague released in a single afternoon in 1996 has killed five billion people by 1997, and the film's future, a sealed underground Philadelphia in 2035, is the ruins. It belongs here because the industrial world does not fall to war or machines but to a laboratory sample carried onto a plane, and because the survivors' only project is reaching back into the world they lost. The paradoxes are the point and are worth stating together: the timeline is a single immutable loop, the message that sends Cole back is Railly's own 1996 voicemail, the bullet in his leg comes from the antique pistol Jose hands him in 1996, and the child who watches him die at the airport grows up to be him, so the plague is caused rather than prevented, and the film's own metaphor for this is Cole watching a movie that never changes. Note the phase anomaly: Cole's 1917 and 1990 scenes count as prehistory by year but are incursions from the branch's own future. Tiers: T2 holds only 2035 because that is the only future the film ever shows, and there is no T1 at all, since this branch ends thirty-nine years after its fork; T4 is real-world background only (the 1889 pandemic). The 2015-2018 television series is a separate continuity and is not counted here.

lineages.title: Fallout
lineages.creator: Tim Cain (Interplay/Black Isle); Bethesda Game Studios from 2008

divergence.label: The Great War
divergence.delta: Real: no nuclear exchange ever comes, the Cold War ends and the twenty-first century's wars stay conventional. Fiction: on Saturday 23 October 2077 the bombs fall in about two hours, 7.54 billion people die, and the Vaults open onto a radioactive forever-1950s wasteland.
divergence.note: The date is uncontested: Fallout's 1997 intro and the Fallout 4 and Fallout 76 loading screens all give Saturday, 23 October 2077. The wider Fallout universe splits from ours after the Second World War in Bethesda's own framing, but this archetype branches on the catastrophe itself, so the War is the fork.

ending.why: Every game ends in a local victory inside a ruined continent, and the refrain holds: war never changes.

events.title: Radioactivity is discovered
events.description: Real history, not fiction: Becquerel finds that uranium emits penetrating rays, and within fifty years the weapon that ends this world exists.
events.note: Real-world background.
events.binWhy: A discovery the rest of the history grows from.

facets.change: matter inert → uranium emits rays

events.title: The timeline splits after the war
events.description: Real history has the transistor arriving in 1947 and technology accelerating into our century, while the fiction's history forks after the Second World War with technology racing ahead while American society stays locked in the 1950s.
events.note: The Fallout 3 manual states the split is 'after World War II' and never dates it precisely; the Fallout Bible, non-canon since 2011, says the same. The widely repeated claim that the transistor was not invented until 2067 is unsupported by canon.
events.binWhy: Technology races ahead of society from this point.

facets.change: post-war → technology races ahead while society freezes

events.title: The Resource Wars begin
events.description: Fuel and uranium run out, the United Nations dissolves and the last manned Moon mission flies as the great powers start seizing what is left.
events.binWhy: A major war starts.

facets.change: scarcity → the powers seize what is left; the UN dissolves

events.title: Project Safehouse: the Vaults
events.description: Vault-Tec wins the contract for the fallout shelters that are really a set of secret sociological experiments on the people sealed inside them, which is the franchise's founding crime.
events.note: The experiment programme is canon across Fallout, Fallout 2, Fallout 3 and Fallout 4; the Vault count is usually given as 122.
events.binWhy: Shelters that are secretly experiments on the people inside them.

facets.change: fear → shelters that are secretly experiments

events.title: The Sino-American War
events.description: China invades Alaska for the last oil and the war runs for eleven years, stripping away the diplomacy that might have prevented the end.
events.binWhy: A major war starts.

facets.change: scarcity → invasion for the last oil; eleven years of war

events.title: The Great War
events.description: Two hours of nuclear exchange on a Saturday morning kill 7.54 billion people, the Vaults seal, and the survivors inherit a wasteland of ruins, ghouls and robots still running their pre-war routines.
events.note: Uncontested across Fallout's intro and the Fallout 4 and 76 loading screens. Earlier the same month the Mariposa mutiny begins the Brotherhood of Steel, so 2077 also carries the wasteland's first institution.
events.binWhy: An attack or disaster kills on a scale that remakes society.

facets.change: cold war → two hours of nuclear exchange

events.title: Reclamation Day
events.description: Vault 76 opens in Appalachia twenty-five years after the bombs, the earliest point at which any Fallout game lets the player out into the wreckage.
events.note: Fallout 76's setting; later updates advance the in-universe clock only to about 2105.
events.binWhy: The shelter opens and its people walk out into the world.

facets.change: sealed → the shelter opens and its people walk out

events.title: The Vault Dweller leaves Vault 13
events.description: The first game: a water-chip failure sends one vault dweller into southern California, where he breaks the Master's Unity and the Cathedral, the moment the wasteland starts producing its own history.
events.binWhy: One person leaves the shelter and starts the wasteland's history.

facets.change: a shelter → one person sent out; the wasteland gets a history

events.title: Fallout 2: the Enclave
events.description: A descendant of the first Vault Dweller crosses a reborn California and destroys the Enclave, the pre-war government's surviving remnant, ending any claim that the old United States still exists.
events.binWhy: A battle or campaign settles the war.

facets.change: the old government's remnant → destroyed

events.title: Fallout 3: the Capital Wasteland
events.description: Two hundred years after the bombs a vault dweller walks out into the ruins of Washington and switches on Project Purity, the first attempt to make the wasteland's water drinkable.
events.binWhy: A shelter-born person walks out into the ruins.

facets.change: a shelter → walks out; the water made drinkable

events.title: Fallout: New Vegas
events.description: The New California Republic and Caesar's Legion fight for Hoover Dam while the strip's proprietor runs a centuries-long plan of his own, the clearest picture of post-war politics the series offers.
events.binWhy: Two powers fight over the dam in a war neither can end.

facets.change: a dam → fought over by two powers

events.title: Fallout 4: the Commonwealth
events.description: A pre-war father wakes from cryogenic sleep into the ruins of Boston and must choose between the Institute's synths, the Brotherhood's airship and the Railroad that frees them.
events.binWhy: A pre-war survivor wakes into the ruins and must choose a side.

facets.change: cryogenic sleep → woken into ruins; a side to choose

events.title: The series reaches the Mojave
events.description: The Amazon series opens in Vault 33, where a wedding between neighbouring vaults turns out to be a raid from the surface, and shows the old world's corporate planning still driving events two hundred and nineteen years after the bombs.
events.note: Seasons 1 (2024) and 2 (2025-26) are both set in 2296; the showrunners have confirmed that no New Vegas ending has been made canon.
events.binWhy: The shelter is opened by a raid and its people are pulled into the world.

facets.change: a sealed shelter → opened by a raid

events.title: Mr. House's colony ships
events.description: In his own projection, New Vegas's proprietor expects to have people in orbit by 2331 and colony ships leaving the solar system by 2381, the branch's stated ambition to leave the ruins behind.
events.note: Conditional dialogue in Fallout: New Vegas, tied to Mr. House's ending: a forecast rather than a depicted event.
events.binWhy: Colony ships are to leave the solar system.

facets.change: ruins → colony ships to leave them behind

events.title: Big Mountain is saved from sonic invasion
events.description: The franchise's furthest dated event: in an Old World Blues ending slide a musical robot builds a counter-frequency that saves Big Mountain from sonic invasion in 2910, eight centuries after the war.
events.note: A conditional, comedic ending slide in a 2011 DLC, and the only dated canon event after 2297; no canon material exists between those two points.
events.binWhy: An invasion is stopped by a counter-frequency.

facets.change: an invasion → stopped by a counter-frequency

lineages.groupingNote: Fallout is the archetype at industrial scale: a two-hour nuclear exchange in the twenty-first century ends the world, and the games then catalogue what grows in it, Vaults that were experiments, a Brotherhood founded by a mutineer, ghouls, robots still polishing floors, and new nations built out of scrap. The fork is the War itself rather than the franchise's earlier, deliberately undated split from our history after the Second World War, because this archetype branches on the catastrophe. Tiers: T2 carries almost the whole branch from 2052 to 2296, because the fiction's entire life sits inside our next three centuries; T3 holds only the real-world wartime split and T4 only real-world background (Becquerel, 1896). T1 exists but is thin and shaky, Mr. House's projected colony ships in 2381 and one Old World Blues ending slide dated 2910, with no dated canon at all between 2297 and 2910; those two entries should be read as the branch's far horizon rather than as depicted history.

lineages.title: The Matrix
lineages.creator: Lana & Lilly Wachowski

divergence.label: The Machine War begins
divergence.delta: Real: no machine nation ever secedes and no sky is ever set on fire; computers stay tools. Fiction: the machines build their own city, humanity answers with nuclear weapons, and the war ends with the sun blotted out and the survivors harvested for power inside a simulation of 1999.
divergence.note: Canonical date text places the Second Renaissance in 2090-2139, and 2139 is the range's end, when the United Nations strikes Zero One; Wikipedia's Animatrix synopsis instead says 2148. Operation Dark Storm, the event that actually ends the human world, is undated on screen.

ending.why: The war between humans and machines ends in an uneasy peace, and the survivors are left free to remake the world they were born into.

events.title: Babbage designs the Analytical Engine
events.description: Real history, not fiction: the first design for a programmable machine, and the real ancestor of the fiction's Machines.
events.note: Real-world background; the fiction is silent before the twenty-first century.
events.binWhy: A discovery the rest of the history grows from.

facets.change: no programmable machine → the first design

events.title: Turing asks whether machines can think
events.description: Real history, not fiction: the imitation game sets the question this franchise answers by giving the machines a nation, an army and a grievance.
events.note: Real-world background.
events.binWhy: A discovery the rest of the history grows from.

facets.change: machines compute → asked whether they think

events.title: The Matrix: the simulated present
events.description: The film is released and its diegetic present is the audience's own 1999, the peak of human civilisation, kept running on a loop to hold the pods docile.
events.note: Morpheus, on screen: 'You believe it's the year 1999... when in fact it's closer to 2199... we honestly don't know.' US release 31 March 1999.
events.binWhy: A real-world publication or release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The Second Renaissance
events.description: A machine called B1-66ER kills the owner who means to scrap it, and the trial, the purge and the Million Machine March that follow end with the machines building their own city, Zero One.
events.note: Canonical date text in The Animatrix and the Matrix comics: 'Zion Archive. World History, 2nd RENAISSANCE, 2090-2139'.
events.binWhy: An artificial mind acts on its own or against its makers.

facets.change: servant machines → a machine kills its owner; a nation of their own

events.title: The Machine War begins
events.description: The United Nations answers Zero One's prosperity with a nuclear strike and the machines retaliate, and the war that ends the human world starts here.
events.note: 2139 is the end of the canonically dated 2090-2139 Second Renaissance range; Wikipedia's Animatrix synopsis says 2148 and fan timelines range into the 2170s.
events.binWhy: A major war starts.

facets.change: a rival prospering → struck with nuclear weapons

events.title: Operation Dark Storm: the sky is scorched
events.description: Humanity's last gambit blots out the sun with nanites to starve the machines of solar power, the machines switch to harvesting human beings, and the industrial world ends under a permanently black sky.
events.note: The event is canonical (The Animatrix) but has no official year; about 2145 places it in the war's first decade. Circulating figures such as 2085 or 2098 are reconstructions.
events.binWhy: The order of society breaks and does not come back.

facets.change: the sun → blotted out to starve the machines; humans farmed

events.title: Neo is extracted: the Machine City era
events.description: The films' present: human beings are grown for power, Zion is the last free city, and the sixth One is offered the choice that resets the cycle.
events.note: Spoken on screen by Morpheus as an approximation. Some tie-in reconstructions instead add five prior One-cycles of about a century each and date the films to roughly 2700.
events.binWhy: The sixth One is found and offered the choice.

facets.change: the pods → the sixth One extracted and offered the choice

events.title: Resurrections: sixty years on
events.description: Sixty years after the truce the Matrix has been rebuilt around Neo and Trinity's grief, and the machines' own civil peace is the only thing keeping the pods running.
events.note: The sixty-year gap is canonical; 2259 is 2199 plus sixty. Cycle-based reconstructions put this film near 2760, which would move the franchise past 2300, but that reading is not supported by on-screen dialogue.
events.binWhy: A jump forward shows what the world became.

facets.change: truce → sixty years on, rebuilt around grief

lineages.groupingNote: The Matrix is the archetype running backwards: the world that ends is a simulation of 1999 kept alive as a power plant, and the ruins the survivors inherit are their own cities under a black sky. Humanity loses a war to its own machines, scorches the sky to win it and is farmed in pods while the last free city hides underground, which is the group's mechanism taken to its logical end. The fork is the Machine War's start at 2139, the close of the canonically dated Second Renaissance range; Operation Dark Storm, which actually ends the human world, is undated on screen and placed at about 2145 here. Tiers: there is no T1, because under the dating the films themselves give (Morpheus's 'closer to 2199' plus the canonical sixty-year gap to Resurrections) this branch stops at 2259; only fan reconstructions that add five prior One-cycles push it past 2300, and that reading contradicts the dialogue. T4 is real-world background only (Babbage, 1834) and T3 holds the simulated 1999 alongside Turing's real 1950.
